brightest-stars-tonight.title: Tonight’s ten brightest stars
brightest-stars-tonight.subtitle: From west to east, starting with those about to set.
brightest-stars-tonight.intro: Tonight the app has picked the ten brightest stars above your horizon. Let your eyes get used to the dark for a few minutes before you start. A very bright point that barely twinkles is probably a planet: the “Moon and planets tonight” tour introduces it.
brightest-stars-tonight.intro.kids: Tonight the app has picked the ten brightest stars in your sky. Give your eyes a few minutes to get used to the dark. A very bright point that barely twinkles is probably a planet: it has its own tour.
brightest-stars-tonight.outro: You now have ten landmarks in tonight’s sky. From one season to the next they drift west and others take their place: repeat this tour in three months. These stars are also the starting point for finding the constellations and the rest of the sky.
brightest-stars-tonight.outro.kids: You now have ten landmarks in tonight’s sky. As the seasons pass they drift west and others take their place. Do this tour again in three months: you will see something new.
brightest-stars-tonight.lead-first: We start in the west, with the star that will set first.
brightest-stars-tonight.lead-first.kids: We start in the west, with the first star to set.
brightest-stars-tonight.lead-last: The last star of the tour, the one furthest east.
brightest-stars-tonight.lead-last.kids: The last star, the one furthest east.
brightest-stars-tonight.lead-low: It is low: look for a clear spot on that side, away from trees and rooftops.
brightest-stars-tonight.lead-low.kids: It is low: find a clear spot on that side, away from trees and rooftops.
brightest-stars-tonight.body-blue: Its light is blue-white: it is one of the hottest stars, far hotter than the Sun. A star’s colour tells the temperature of its surface, from red for the coolest to blue for the hottest.
brightest-stars-tonight.body-blue.kids: Its light is blue-white. It is one of the hottest stars, far hotter than the Sun. A star’s colour shows its temperature: red for the coolest, blue for the hottest.
brightest-stars-tonight.body-white: Its light is white, sometimes with a hint of blue: its surface is hotter than the Sun’s. In binoculars it stays a point, because even the biggest stars are too far away to show a disc.
brightest-stars-tonight.body-white.kids: Its light is white, sometimes a little blue. Its surface is hotter than the Sun’s. Even in binoculars it stays a point: stars are too far away to show a round disc.
brightest-stars-tonight.body-yellow: Its light runs from yellow-white to yellow, close to the Sun’s. From this far away, our Sun would look like this point, only fainter. Look straight at it: the centre of the eye is where colours are seen.
brightest-stars-tonight.body-yellow.kids: Its light is yellow or yellow-white, close to the Sun’s. From this far away, our Sun would look like this point, only fainter. Look straight at it: the centre of your eye sees colours best.
brightest-stars-tonight.body-orange: Its light is orange: its surface is cooler than the Sun’s. It is often a giant, an old star that has swollen a great deal. In binoculars its colour stands out even better.
brightest-stars-tonight.body-orange.kids: Its light is orange: its surface is cooler than the Sun’s. It is often a giant, an old star that has swollen. In binoculars, its colour stands out even better.
brightest-stars-tonight.body-red: Its light is orange-red, one of the reddest of the bright stars. It is a cool, immense star near the end of its life. In binoculars, if you blur the focus a little, the colour becomes vivid.
brightest-stars-tonight.body-red.kids: Its light is orange-red, one of the reddest in the sky. It is a huge, cool star, close to the end of its life. In binoculars, blur the focus a little: the colour gets stronger.
moon-and-planets-tonight.title: Moon and planets tonight
moon-and-planets-tonight.subtitle: What is well placed tonight, from west to east.
moon-and-planets-tonight.intro: Tonight the app has kept only the Moon and the planets that are well above your horizon. Planets hardly twinkle, unlike stars: that is the first clue to recognising them. Binoculars held steady, against a wall or a railing, are enough for most stops.
moon-and-planets-tonight.intro.kids: Tonight the Moon and the planets are well up in your sky. A planet hardly twinkles, unlike a star: that is the first clue to spotting one. Binoculars braced against a wall or a railing are almost always enough.
moon-and-planets-tonight.outro: The planets move slowly against the stars from one week to the next. Come back in a few days: the Moon will have changed shape and place, and so will the tour. Note what you saw in the Journal so you can compare.
moon-and-planets-tonight.outro.kids: The planets drift slowly against the stars from one week to the next. Come back in a few days: the Moon will have changed shape and place. Write down what you saw in the Journal, so you can compare.
moon-and-planets-tonight.lead-low: This stop is low on the horizon, where the thick air makes the image shimmer: look for a clear spot on that side.
moon-and-planets-tonight.lead-low.kids: It is low, where the thick air makes the image shimmer. Find a clear spot on that side.
moon-and-planets-tonight.body-moon-cresc: A thin crescent, lit on the side where the Sun has set. Look at the dark part: it glows faintly, lit by sunlight reflected back by the Earth. In binoculars, craters show along the boundary between day and night.

A thin crescent, turned towards where the Sun has set. Look at the dark part: it glows faintly, because the Earth sends some light back. In binoculars, craters show along the line between day and night.
moon-and-planets-tonight.body-moon-quart: The Moon is half lit, the best time to see its relief. In binoculars, follow the boundary between day and night: craters are picked out there by long shadows. Through a telescope, the lowest magnification is enough to start with.

The Moon is half lit, the best time to see its craters and mountains. In binoculars, follow the line between day and night. Craters have long shadows there. Through a telescope, the lowest magnification is enough to start.
moon-and-planets-tonight.body-moon-gibbo: The Moon is more than half lit and its light is starting to wash out the sky. In binoculars, look for the large dark plains, the seas, and the craters near the edge that is still in shadow.
The Moon is more than half lit. In binoculars, look for the big dark plains, called seas. Look for craters too, near the edge that is still in shadow.
moon-and-planets-tonight.body-moon-full: The full Moon, opposite the Sun: the relief disappears, because the light falls straight onto the ground. Look instead for the bright streaks that spread from some craters, like rays. Through a telescope its light is dazzling: look at it only briefly.
It is the full Moon, opposite the Sun. Its craters look flat, because the light falls straight down on them. Look for the bright streaks spreading from some craters, like rays. Through a telescope it is dazzling, so only look for a moment.
moon-and-planets-tonight.body-moon-wanin: The Moon is waning and rises later each evening. It stays very bright: in binoculars, follow the boundary between day and night, where shadows still emphasise the relief.
The Moon is waning: each evening it rises a little later. It stays very bright. In binoculars, follow the line between day and night, where shadows show the craters.
moon-and-planets-tonight.body-mercury: Mercury, the closest planet to the Sun, always stays low in the twilight. It is a yellowish point, often hard to see: sweep the horizon with binoculars, but never before the Sun has set.
moon-and-planets-tonight.body-mercury.ki: Mercury, the planet closest to the Sun, always stays low in the twilight. It is a yellowish point, hard to find. Sweep the horizon with binoculars, but never before the Sun has set.
moon-and-planets-tonight.body-venus: Venus, the brightest object after the Moon, is impossible to miss. Through a telescope or with good, steadied binoculars, it shows a phase, like a small Moon, because we see part of its face in shadow.
moon-and-planets-tonight.body-venus.kids: Venus is the brightest object after the Moon: you cannot miss it. It has phases, like a small Moon. With good binoculars held steady or a telescope, you can see part of its face in shadow.
moon-and-planets-tonight.body-mars: Mars is recognised by its orange colour and steady light. Its brightness changes a lot from one year to the next, depending on its distance from the Earth. Through a telescope, you need a steady sky to make out a polar cap or dark patches.
moon-and-planets-tonight.body-mars.kids: You can recognise Mars by its orange colour and steady light. Its brightness changes from year to year, depending on how far it is from the Earth. Through a telescope, when the air is steady, try to spot a white polar cap or dark patches.
moon-and-planets-tonight.body-jupiter: Jupiter shines with a strong white light. In well-steadied binoculars, look for small points in a line on either side: its largest moons. Through a telescope, two dark bands cross its disc.
moon-and-planets-tonight.body-jupiter.ki: Jupiter shines with a strong white light. With binoculars held steady, look for small points in a line on either side: its largest moons. Through a telescope, two dark bands cross its disc.
moon-and-planets-tonight.body-saturn: Saturn is a pale yellow, steady point. Through a telescope, even a small one, its rings can be seen from medium magnification: it is often the highlight of a first evening. Their tilt changes over the years.
moon-and-planets-tonight.body-saturn.kid: Saturn is a pale yellow, steady point. Through a telescope, even a small one, its rings show up at medium magnification. Their tilt changes over the years. It is often the highlight of a first evening.
moon-and-planets-tonight.body-uranus: Uranus is at the limit of the naked eye: in binoculars it is a point that looks like a faint star. Through a telescope it becomes a tiny blue-green disc. The pointing aid helps you find it among the neighbouring stars.
moon-and-planets-tonight.body-uranus.kid: Uranus is only just visible to the naked eye. In binoculars, it looks like a faint star. Through a telescope, it is a tiny blue-green disc. The pointing aid guides you to it among the neighbouring stars.
moon-and-planets-tonight.body-neptune: Neptune needs a telescope: it is a bluish point, barely bigger than a star, even at high magnification. Finding it is already a success. The pointing aid helps you tell it from the neighbouring stars.
moon-and-planets-tonight.body-neptune.ki: Neptune needs a telescope. It is a bluish point, barely bigger than a star, even at high magnification. Just finding it is a real achievement. The pointing aid guides you among the neighbouring stars.
season-constellations.title: The constellations of the season
season-constellations.subtitle: The great figures of tonight’s sky, from one to the next.
season-constellations.intro: A constellation is found step by step: each stop starts from the previous one. Hold out your arm: a closed fist covers about 10 degrees of sky, an open hand about 20. Faint stars need a dark sky and eyes that have had at least a quarter of an hour to adapt to the dark.
season-constellations.intro.kids: Each stop starts from the previous one: you find the constellations step by step. Hold out your arm. A closed fist covers about 10 degrees of sky, an open hand about 20. To see faint stars you need a dark sky and a quarter of an hour for your eyes to adapt.
season-constellations.outro: You can now move from one constellation to the next without a chart. In three months, the early-evening sky will have turned by a quarter: repeat this tour and you will find it has changed with the season. Deep-sky objects hide in these figures, and the telescope tour starts from the same landmarks.
season-constellations.outro.kids: You can now move from one constellation to the next without a chart. In three months, the early-evening sky will have turned by a quarter. Repeat this tour: it will have changed. Deep-sky objects hide in these figures, and the telescope tour starts from the same landmarks.
season-constellations.north-winter.subti: Around Orion, the region richest in bright stars.
season-constellations.north-winter.ori: Facing south, halfway up the sky, look for three stars close together in a line, in the middle of a big rectangle of four bright stars. At the upper left, Betelgeuse is orange; at the lower right, Rigel is blue-white. Orion appears in the evening in late autumn and disappears in spring: it is the landmark of winter.
season-constellations.north-winter.ori.k: Facing south, halfway up the sky, look for three stars close together in a line: the belt of a giant called Orion. Around it, four bright stars draw a big rectangle. At the upper left, Betelgeuse is orange. At the lower right, Rigel is blue-white. Orion is the landmark of winter.
season-constellations.north-winter.tau: Follow Orion’s belt up and to the right for an open hand’s width: you reach Aldebaran, an orange star. Keep going in the same direction to a small cloud of close-set stars, the Pleiades. How many can you count with the naked eye? Six or seven usually, dozens in binoculars.
season-constellations.north-winter.tau.k: Follow Orion’s belt up and to the right, one open hand’s width, to Aldebaran, an orange star. Keep going the same way to a small cloud of close-set stars, the Pleiades. How many can you count with the naked eye? Six or seven usually, dozens in binoculars.
season-constellations.north-winter.aur: Above Taurus, almost overhead, shines a yellow star: Capella. The lower corner of the Auriga figure is also a horn of Taurus; long ago, that corner star was counted in both constellations. In binoculars, sweep slowly across the inside of the figure: the Milky Way there is sprinkled with small clusters.
season-constellations.north-winter.aur.k: Above Taurus, almost overhead, shines a yellow star: Capella, in Auriga. In binoculars, sweep slowly across the inside of the figure. The Milky Way there is sprinkled with small star clusters.
season-constellations.north-winter.gem: To the left of Capella, towards the east, two stars of equal brightness shine side by side: Castor and Pollux. Pollux is a little orange, Castor white; the difference shows better in binoculars. From these two stars, two lines of fainter stars run down towards Orion, like two figures with an arm over each other’s shoulder.
season-constellations.north-winter.gem.k: To the left of Capella, towards the east, two stars of equal brightness shine side by side: Castor and Pollux. Pollux is a little orange, Castor white. Two lines of fainter stars run down towards Orion. They look like two people, each with an arm around the other’s shoulders.
season-constellations.north-winter.cmi: Below Pollux, an open hand’s width down, a bright star stands almost alone: Procyon. In binoculars, compare its colour with that of Sirius, the next stop: Procyon is a little more yellow.
season-constellations.north-winter.cmi.k: Below Pollux, an open hand’s width down, a bright star stands almost alone: Procyon. In binoculars, compare its colour with Sirius, the next stop. Procyon is a little more yellow.
season-constellations.north-winter.cma: Go back to the bottom of Orion: a little to the left, the brightest star of the night sky, Sirius, cannot be missed. Fairly low, it often twinkles in all colours, because the unsteady air near the horizon splits its light. The dog’s body runs down below it, towards the horizon.
season-constellations.north-winter.cma.k: Go back to the bottom of Orion, a little to the left. Sirius, the brightest star of the night sky, cannot be missed. When it is low, it twinkles in every colour, because the moving air splits up its light. The body of the great dog runs down below it.
season-constellations.north-winter.lep: Below Rigel, a fist’s width down, a small group of faint stars makes up Lepus, the Hare. You need a dark sky and a clear southern horizon to see its shape, two ears pricked up towards Orion. It is a good gauge of your sky tonight: if you see it easily, the night is a good one.
season-constellations.north-winter.lep.k: Below Rigel, a fist’s width down, a few faint stars draw Lepus, the Hare, with two ears pricked up towards Orion. You need a dark sky and a clear southern horizon. If you see it easily, your sky is very good.
season-constellations.north-winter.winte: Step back and look at the whole region: Sirius, Procyon, Pollux, Capella, Aldebaran and Rigel form an immense hexagon, with Betelgeuse near the centre. It is the corner of the sky richest in bright stars of the whole year. On a moonless night, far from cities, the Milky Way crosses it, pale, from Capella to Sirius.

Step back and look at the whole region. Sirius, Procyon, Pollux, Capella, Aldebaran and Rigel form an immense hexagon. Betelgeuse is near the centre. No other corner of the sky has so many bright stars, all year round. On a moonless night, far from cities, the Milky Way crosses it, from Capella to Sirius.
season-constellations.north-spring.subti: From Ursa Major towards the south, following its stars.
season-constellations.north-spring.uma: Facing north, very high, almost overhead, seven stars trace the Big Dipper, upside down. It is the best-known part of Ursa Major; its other, fainter stars make up the head and paws. In the middle of the handle, good eyesight separates two close stars, Mizar and Alcor: an old eyesight test.
season-constellations.north-spring.uma.k: Facing north, very high, almost overhead, seven stars trace the Big Dipper, upside down. It is part of Ursa Major. Look closely at the middle of the handle: two very close stars, Mizar and Alcor. Telling them apart was an eyesight test in the old days.
season-constellations.north-spring.umi: Take the two stars on the rim of the Big Dipper’s bowl, opposite the handle, and extend the gap between them five times towards the north: you find the pole star. It is not very bright, but it hardly moves: the whole sky turns around it. Its height above the horizon is roughly equal to the latitude of your place.
season-constellations.north-spring.umi.k: Take the two stars on the rim of the Big Dipper’s bowl, opposite the handle. Extend the gap between them five times towards the north: you find the pole star. It is not very bright, but it hardly moves. The whole sky turns around it. The further north you live, the higher it stands.
season-constellations.north-spring.leo: Go back to the same two stars of the Big Dipper’s bowl and extend them the other way, towards the south, over two to three open hands: you reach Leo. Look for a lion lying down, head turned to the west and tail to the east. It is one of the few constellations that really look like what they represent.
season-constellations.north-spring.leo.k: Go back to the same two stars of the bowl and extend the line the other way, towards the south, for two or three open hands. You reach Leo. Look for a big animal lying down, head to the west and tail to the east. It really looks like what it is meant to be.
season-constellations.north-spring.cnc: Between Leo’s head and Pollux, lower towards the west, the sky looks empty: this is Cancer. Point binoculars at the middle of that gap: dozens of stars appear at once in the field. The ancients saw a manger there, with two donkeys beside it, two neighbouring stars.
season-constellations.north-spring.cnc.k: Between Leo’s head and Pollux, lower towards the west, the sky looks empty: this is Cancer. Point binoculars at the middle of that gap. Dozens of stars appear at once. Long ago, people saw a manger there, with two donkeys beside it: two nearby stars.
season-constellations.north-spring.com: Start from Leo’s tail and go north-east for a fist and a half: a scattering of faint stars floats there, with no clear figure. Binoculars show a spray of stars, like hair spread out. In that direction we look out of the disc of our galaxy, towards thousands of distant galaxies.
season-constellations.north-spring.com.k: Start from Leo’s tail and go north-east for a fist and a half. A scattering of faint stars floats there, with no clear figure. In binoculars it is a spray of stars, like hair spread out. Here we look out of the disc of our galaxy, towards thousands of distant galaxies.
season-constellations.north-spring.boo: Keep going east: an orange star shines alone, high in the sky, Arcturus. Its fainter figure rises above it towards the north. It is the brightest star of the whole northern half of the sky, and its colour shows well to the naked eye.
season-constellations.north-spring.boo.k: Keep going east: an orange star shines alone, high in the sky. It is Arcturus. Its fainter figure rises above it towards the north. It is the brightest star of the northern half of the sky, and its colour shows well to the naked eye.
season-constellations.north-spring.vir: From Arcturus, go down towards the south-west for a little under two open hands: lower down, a blue-white star shines, Spica. The rest of Virgo is a large faint figure, hard to follow under a city sky. It is the largest constellation of the zodiac, and the second largest in the whole sky.
season-constellations.north-spring.vir.k: From Arcturus, go down towards the south-west for a little under two open hands. A blue-white star shines lower down: Spica. The rest of Virgo is faint and hard to follow under a city sky. It is the largest constellation of the zodiac.
season-constellations.north-spring.crv: West of Spica, a fist and a half away, four medium-bright stars form a small square sail, low towards the south. This is Corvus, easy to spot even under an average sky, because nothing bright surrounds it. Its two upper stars point to Spica.
season-constellations.north-spring.crv.k: West of Spica, a fist and a half away, four medium-bright stars form a small square sail. This is Corvus, low towards the south. Nothing bright surrounds it, so it is easy to spot. Its two upper stars point to Spica.
season-constellations.north-summer.subti: From the Summer Triangle to Scorpius, along the Milky Way.
season-constellations.north-summer.lyr: Almost overhead, the brightest star is Vega, white with a slight blue tint. Beside it, to the east, a faint star looks double in binoculars. Through a telescope, each of the two splits again: this is the Double Double, a classic of observing evenings.
season-constellations.north-summer.lyr.k: Almost overhead, the brightest star is Vega, white with a slight blue tint. Beside it, to the east, a faint star looks double in binoculars. Through a telescope, each of the two splits again: this is the Double Double.
season-constellations.north-summer.cyg: From Vega, go east for an open hand’s width: Deneb, less bright, marks the tail of a great bird flying south along the Milky Way. Its wings spread across; its head is a faint star, far ahead, towards Altair. Through a telescope, that star in the head, Albireo, is a gold and blue pair, one of the most beautiful in the sky.
season-constellations.north-summer.cyg.k: From Vega, go east for an open hand’s width. Deneb, less bright, is the tail of a great bird. It flies south along the Milky Way, wings spread. Its head is a faint star, far ahead towards Altair: Albireo. Through a telescope, it is a pair of stars, one gold, one blue.
season-constellations.north-summer.aql: Follow the Swan’s neck south, beyond Albireo: a bright star between two fainter ones is Altair, in Aquila. Vega, Deneb and Altair form the Summer Triangle, a landmark for evenings from July to October. That name is the northern hemisphere’s: in the south, these three stars are a winter landmark, low on the horizon.
season-constellations.north-summer.aql.k: Follow the Swan’s neck south, beyond Albireo. A bright star between two fainter ones is Altair, in Aquila. Vega, Deneb and Altair form the Summer Triangle, a landmark from July to October. In the southern hemisphere, it is a winter landmark, low on the horizon.
season-constellations.north-summer.milky: Turn off every light and look at the pale band crossing the Summer Triangle from north to south: this is the Milky Way, our galaxy seen from the inside. In Cygnus, a dark zone splits it in two, a cloud of dust that hides the stars behind it. Lower towards the south, it widens and shines brighter: we are looking towards the centre of the galaxy.

Turn off every light and look at the pale band crossing the Summer Triangle from north to south. It is the Milky Way, our galaxy seen from the inside. In Cygnus, a cloud of dust splits it in two. Lower towards the south, it widens and shines brighter: we are looking towards the centre of the galaxy.
season-constellations.north-summer.del: Go back to Altair and move up about a fist towards the north-east: a small tight figure, sharp even under a suburban sky, waits there. It is Delphinus, which fits entirely in the field of binoculars. Two of its stars have strange names, Sualocin and Rotanev: read backwards, they give the Latinised name of a 19th-century astronomer.
season-constellations.north-summer.del.k: Go back to Altair and climb about a fist towards the north-east. A small, tight figure, sharp even from the suburbs, waits there: Delphinus. It fits entirely in the field of binoculars. Two of its stars have strange names, Sualocin and Rotanev. Read backwards, they spell the Latin name of a 19th-century astronomer.
season-constellations.north-summer.her: Go back to Vega and head west for an open hand’s width: four medium-bright stars form a trapezium, the centre of Hercules. On the west side of the trapezium, in binoculars, a small fuzzy ball appears. It is a cluster of several hundred thousand stars, seen as a single flake.
season-constellations.north-summer.her.k: Go back to Vega and head west for an open hand’s width. Four medium-bright stars form a trapezium, the centre of Hercules. On its west side, binoculars show a small fuzzy ball. It is a cluster of several hundred thousand stars, that looks like one tiny snowflake.
season-constellations.north-summer.crb: Keep going west, halfway between Hercules and Arcturus: a small arc of stars looks like a diadem. This is Corona Borealis, compact and easy once spotted. Its brightest star, at the centre, also bears the Latin name Gemma, “the jewel”.
season-constellations.north-summer.crb.k: Keep going west, halfway between Hercules and Arcturus. A small arc of stars looks like an open crown: Corona Borealis. Its brightest star, at the centre, also has a Latin name, Gemma, “the jewel”.
season-constellations.north-summer.sco: Turn to the south, fairly low: a red-orange star shines in the middle of a line of stars, Antares, the heart of Scorpius. Depending on your latitude, its curled tail stays partly below the horizon. Antares is so large that, in the Sun’s place, it would swallow the orbit of Mars.
season-constellations.north-summer.sco.k: Turn south, fairly low. A red-orange star shines in the middle of a line of stars: Antares, the heart of Scorpius. Depending on your latitude, its curled tail stays partly below the horizon. Antares is so big that, in the Sun’s place, it would swallow Mars’s orbit.
season-constellations.north-summer.sgr: East of Scorpius, still low towards the south, eight stars trace a teapot, with its spout, lid and handle. The Milky Way rises from it like steam, brighter here than anywhere else. In binoculars, sweep slowly above the spout: star clouds, clusters and nebulae follow one another.
season-constellations.north-summer.sgr.k: East of Scorpius, still low towards the south, eight stars trace a teapot. Look for its spout, lid and handle. The Milky Way rises from it like steam, brighter here than anywhere else. In binoculars, sweep slowly above the spout: you pass star clouds, clusters and nebulae.
season-constellations.north-autumn.subti: From Cassiopeia to the Great Square of Pegasus, then south.
season-constellations.north-autumn.cas: Facing north, high in the sky, five medium-bright stars trace a W, or an M depending on the hour. This is Cassiopeia, always visible at mid northern latitudes: it circles the pole star without ever setting. In binoculars, sweep around the W: clusters of stars appear everywhere.
season-constellations.north-autumn.cas.k: Facing north, high in the sky, five medium-bright stars trace a W, or an M depending on the hour. This is Cassiopeia. From mid northern latitudes, it circles the pole star without ever setting. In binoculars, sweep around the W: clusters of stars appear everywhere.
season-constellations.north-autumn.cep: Between Cassiopeia and the pole star, a little to the west, five fainter stars form Cepheus. You need a fairly dark sky to see it whole. Near the base of the figure, look in binoculars for a deep red star: the Garnet Star, one of the reddest visible to the naked eye.
season-constellations.north-autumn.cep.k: Between Cassiopeia and the pole star, a little to the west, five fainter stars form Cepheus. You need a fairly dark sky to see it whole. Near its base, look in binoculars for a deep red star: the Garnet Star.
season-constellations.north-autumn.peg: From Cassiopeia, go down towards the south, high in the sky: four stars of equal brightness form a big empty square, a fist and a half wide. This is the body of Pegasus, the winged horse, flying head down. Count the stars visible inside the square: none or almost none under a city sky, many more under a country sky.
season-constellations.north-autumn.peg.k: From Cassiopeia, go down towards the south, high in the sky. Four stars of equal brightness form a big empty square, a fist and a half wide. It is the body of Pegasus, the winged horse, flying head down. Count the stars inside the square: almost none under a city sky, many more in the country.
season-constellations.north-autumn.and: From the north-east corner of the square, follow a chain of stars east to the second bright star, Mirach. From there, climb north past two fainter stars and a little beyond: a pale oval patch appears, visible to the naked eye under a dark sky, easily in binoculars. This is the Andromeda Galaxy, one of the most distant objects the eye can see without an instrument.
season-constellations.north-autumn.and.k: From the north-east corner of the square, follow a chain of stars east to the second bright star, Mirach. Climb north past two fainter stars and a little beyond. A pale oval patch appears: the Andromeda Galaxy. You can see it with the naked eye under a dark sky, and easily in binoculars. Its light set out more than two million years ago.
season-constellations.north-autumn.per: Continue the Andromeda chain to the north-east: an arc of stars rises along the Milky Way, this is Perseus. In binoculars, the region around its main star, Mirfak, is a swarm of bluish stars. In Perseus, the star Algol dims for a few hours, almost every three days, when a companion star passes in front of it.
season-constellations.north-autumn.per.k: Continue the Andromeda chain to the north-east. An arc of stars rises along the Milky Way: this is Perseus. In binoculars, the region around its main star, Mirfak, is full of bluish stars. The star Algol dims for a few hours, almost every three days, when a companion star passes in front of it.
season-constellations.north-autumn.tri: Just under the Andromeda chain, three faint stars form a narrow, elongated triangle. It is one of the smallest figures of the tour, but one of the simplest. Under a very dark sky, a barely visible glow floats between Triangulum and Mirach: another galaxy, at the limit of the naked eye.
season-constellations.north-autumn.tri.k: Just under the Andromeda chain, three faint stars form a narrow triangle. It is one of the smallest figures of the tour, and one of the simplest. Under a very dark sky, a glow floats between Triangulum and Mirach. It is another galaxy, at the limit of the naked eye.
season-constellations.north-autumn.ari: A little lower towards the south-east, two fairly bright stars and a fainter third form a short bent line: this is Aries. A little over two thousand years ago, the Sun stood here at the spring equinox; that point has since slipped into Pisces. It is the effect of a slow wobble of the Earth’s axis, which makes one turn in about 26,000 years.
season-constellations.north-autumn.ari.k: A little lower towards the south-east, two fairly bright stars and a fainter third form a short bent line: Aries. A little over two thousand years ago, the Sun stood here on the day spring begins. That point has since slipped into Pisces. The Earth’s axis wobbles slowly, like a spinning top. One turn takes about 26,000 years.
season-constellations.north-autumn.psa: To finish, look low to the south, under the square of Pegasus: a bright star stands alone there, Fomalhaut. Nothing bright surrounds it, hence its nickname, the lone star of autumn. From mid northern latitudes it never climbs high: a clear southern horizon helps a lot.
season-constellations.north-autumn.psa.k: To finish, look low to the south, under the square of Pegasus. A bright star stands alone there: Fomalhaut. Nothing bright surrounds it, so it is called the lone star of autumn. From mid northern latitudes it never climbs high. You need a clear southern horizon.
season-constellations.south-summer.subti: From Orion, upside down, to the Large Magellanic Cloud.
season-constellations.south-summer.ori: Facing north, halfway up, three stars close together in a line form the centre of Orion, upside down as seen from here. Many see a saucepan: the three stars are its base, and the sword rising above is the handle. Rigel, blue-white, is at the upper left, and Betelgeuse, orange, at the lower right.
season-constellations.south-summer.ori.k: Facing north, halfway up, three stars close together in a line form the centre of Orion, upside down as seen from here. Many see a saucepan: the three stars are the base, the sword the handle. Rigel, blue-white, is at the upper left. Betelgeuse, orange, is at the lower right.
season-constellations.south-summer.tau: Follow the three belt stars to the left and down for an open hand’s width: you reach Aldebaran, orange. Keep going in the same direction to a small cloud of close-set stars, low towards the north. How many can you count with the naked eye? Six or seven usually, dozens in binoculars.
season-constellations.south-summer.tau.k: Follow the three belt stars to the left and down for an open hand’s width, to orange Aldebaran. Keep going the same way, low towards the north, to a small cloud of close-set stars. How many can you count with the naked eye? Six or seven usually, dozens in binoculars.
season-constellations.south-summer.cma: Go back to the centre of Orion and follow the belt the other way, up and to the right: Sirius, the brightest star of the night sky, shines almost overhead. At that height it twinkles little and shows its true colour, a pure white. The rest of the dog extends above it, towards the zenith.
season-constellations.south-summer.cma.k: Go back to the centre of Orion and follow the belt the other way, up and to the right. Sirius, the brightest star of the night sky, shines almost overhead. Up there it twinkles little and shows its true colour, a pure white. The rest of the great dog stretches out above it.
season-constellations.south-summer.lep: Above Rigel, towards the zenith, a small group of faint stars makes up Lepus, the Hare. From the southern hemisphere it passes high in the sky and is much easier to see than from the north. A dark sky helps you follow its shape, two ears turned towards Orion.
season-constellations.south-summer.lep.k: Above Rigel, towards the zenith, a few faint stars draw Lepus, the Hare. From here it passes high and is much easier to see than from the north. A dark sky helps you follow its shape, two ears turned towards Orion.
season-constellations.south-summer.col: Continue in the same direction, a fist beyond Lepus: a small figure of medium-bright stars, Columba, the Dove, passes almost through the zenith. Under an average sky, only its two main stars show. Under a truly dark sky, the outline of a bird appears.
season-constellations.south-summer.col.k: Continue the same way, a fist beyond Lepus. A small figure of medium-bright stars passes almost overhead: Columba, the Dove. Under an average sky, you only see its two main stars. Under a dark sky, you can make out a bird.
season-constellations.south-summer.car: Further south, high in the sky, a very bright star stands out: Canopus, the second brightest of the night sky. From mid southern latitudes it circles the pole and barely sets. The rest of Carina extends east along the Milky Way, still low tonight on that side.
season-constellations.south-summer.car.k: Further south, high up, a very bright star stands out: Canopus, second brightest of the night. From mid southern latitudes, it circles the pole and barely sets. It is part of Carina, a great ship’s keel. That figure stretches east along the Milky Way.
season-constellations.south-summer.dor: Between Canopus and the south pole, a little to the west, a pale patch of light floats apart from the Milky Way, like a piece broken off: the Large Magellanic Cloud. You need a moonless sky, far from cities, to see it with the naked eye; in binoculars it teems with small nebulae and clusters. Its light has travelled for about 160,000 years to reach you.
season-constellations.south-summer.dor.k: Between Canopus and the south pole, a little to the west, a pale patch of light floats apart from the Milky Way. It looks like a piece broken off: the Large Magellanic Cloud. You need a moonless sky, far from cities, to see it with the naked eye. In binoculars it teems with nebulae and clusters. Its light has travelled about 160,000 years to reach you.
season-constellations.south-summer.eri: From the Large Cloud, go west by a little more than an open hand: a bright, isolated star, Achernar, ends a long river of faint stars. This river zigzags up to near Rigel, across a large part of the visible sky. South of latitude 33 degrees, Achernar never sets.
season-constellations.south-summer.eri.k: From the Large Cloud, go west by a little more than an open hand. A bright, isolated star, Achernar, ends a long river of faint stars. The river zigzags up to near Rigel. South of latitude 33 degrees, Achernar never sets.
season-constellations.south-autumn.subti: From the Southern Cross north, to Leo.
season-constellations.south-autumn.cru: Facing south, high in the sky, a small cross of four bright stars stands on the Milky Way: the Southern Cross. Extend its long axis, from the top to the foot, by four and a half times its length: you arrive near the south celestial pole, where no bright star marks the spot. The top star is orange; the other three are blue-white.
season-constellations.south-autumn.cru.k: Facing south, high in the sky, four bright stars draw a small cross on the Milky Way: the Southern Cross. The top star is orange, the other three are blue-white. Follow the cross from top to foot, then keep going four and a half times that far. You arrive near the south celestial pole. No bright star marks the spot.
season-constellations.south-autumn.cen: To the left of the Cross, two very bright stars side by side point towards it: these are the Pointers, the foot of Centaurus. The rest of the figure rises towards the zenith. Up there, look for a slightly fuzzy star: in binoculars it becomes a ball of light, the Omega Centauri cluster.
season-constellations.south-autumn.cen.k: To the left of the Cross, two very bright stars side by side point towards it: the Pointers, the foot of Centaurus. The rest of the figure rises towards the zenith. Up there, look for a slightly fuzzy star. In binoculars it becomes a ball of light: the Omega Centauri cluster.
season-constellations.south-autumn.mus: Just under the Cross, a small figure of four or five medium-bright stars forms Musca. Against the flank of the Cross, the black patch of the Coalsack punches a hole in the Milky Way. Several Aboriginal peoples of Australia see in it the head of an emu, whose long dark body stretches through the Milky Way to Scorpius.
season-constellations.south-autumn.mus.k: Just under the Cross, four or five medium-bright stars form Musca. Against the flank of the Cross, a black patch punches a hole in the Milky Way: the Coalsack. Several Aboriginal peoples of Australia see the head of an emu in it. Its long dark body stretches through the Milky Way to Scorpius.
season-constellations.south-autumn.car: Follow the Milky Way west, to the right of the Cross: a glow spreads there, spotted with black in binoculars, the Carina Nebula. At its heart, the star Eta Carinae was for a time the second brightest in the sky, around 1843, before almost vanishing from naked-eye view. It remains one of the most massive stars known.
season-constellations.south-autumn.car.k: Follow the Milky Way west, to the right of the Cross. A glow spreads there, spotted with black in binoculars: the Carina Nebula. At its heart, the star Eta Carinae was the second brightest in the sky around 1843, before almost vanishing from naked-eye view. It is one of the heaviest stars we know.
season-constellations.south-autumn.vel: Continue west: four stars form a cross larger and paler than the real one; only the real one has two Pointers beside it. North of this false cross, Vela unfurls over the Milky Way. In binoculars, sweep the region: it is dotted with small clusters, including a bright group around a bluish star.
season-constellations.south-autumn.vel.k: Continue west: four stars form a cross larger and paler than the real one. This is the False Cross: only the real one has two Pointers beside it. North of it, Vela unfurls over the Milky Way. In binoculars, sweep the region: it is dotted with small clusters.
season-constellations.south-autumn.leo: Now turn to the north: halfway up, a bright white star, Regulus, ends the figure of a lion lying down, upside down as seen from here. Leo’s head is to the lower left, its tail to the right. In April, Leo can be seen in the evening from both hemispheres; from the north, it passes high and the right way up.
season-constellations.south-autumn.leo.k: Now turn to the north. Halfway up, a bright white star, Regulus, ends the figure of a lion lying down, upside down as seen from here. Its head is to the lower left, its tail to the right. In April, Leo can be seen in the evening from both hemispheres. From the north, it passes high, the right way up.
season-constellations.south-autumn.vir: To the right of Leo, higher towards the north-east, a blue-white star shines alone: Spica. The rest of Virgo, faint, spreads between it and Leo’s tail. Spica is almost on the Moon’s path: the Moon sometimes passes in front of it and hides it for nearly an hour.
season-constellations.south-autumn.vir.k: To the right of Leo, higher towards the north-east, a blue-white star shines alone: Spica. The rest of Virgo, faint, spreads between it and Leo’s tail. Sometimes the Moon passes in front of Spica and hides it for nearly an hour.
season-constellations.south-autumn.crv: Between Spica and the Cross, almost overhead, four medium-bright stars form a small square sail: Corvus. Nothing bright surrounds it, so it is easy to spot, even under an average sky. Its two stars turned towards Spica form an arrow pointing to it.
season-constellations.south-autumn.crv.k: Between Spica and the Cross, almost overhead, four medium-bright stars form a small square sail: Corvus. Nothing bright surrounds it, so it is easy to spot. Its two stars turned towards Spica make an arrow pointing to it.
season-constellations.south-winter.subti: Scorpius overhead and the heart of the Milky Way.
season-constellations.south-winter.sco: Look up: almost at the zenith, a long hooked line of stars crosses the sky, with a red-orange star in the middle, Antares. This is Scorpius, whole and spectacular from the southern hemisphere. It is one of the few constellations that really look like what they represent, claws, body and sting included.
season-constellations.south-winter.sco.k: Look up: almost at the zenith, a long hooked line of stars crosses the sky. In the middle shines a red-orange star: Antares. This is Scorpius, whole and spectacular from the southern hemisphere. Look for its claws, body and sting.
season-constellations.south-winter.sgr: East of Scorpius’s tail, eight stars trace a teapot, upside down as seen from here, its spout turned towards Scorpius. The Milky Way escapes from it like steam, wider and brighter here than anywhere else. In binoculars, sweep around the spout: star clouds, clusters and nebulae follow one another.
season-constellations.south-winter.sgr.k: East of Scorpius’s tail, eight stars trace a teapot, upside down from here, with its spout turned towards Scorpius. The Milky Way rises from it like steam, wider and brighter than anywhere else. In binoculars, sweep around the spout. You pass star clouds, clusters and nebulae.
season-constellations.south-winter.milky: Turn off every light and look at the Milky Way above you, from Sagittarius to the Southern Cross. It is thick, mottled with dark bands: clouds of dust that hide the stars behind them. It is the best time of year to see it: the brightest part of the galaxy passes high in the evening sky.

Turn off every light and look at the Milky Way above you, from Sagittarius to the Southern Cross. It is thick, mottled with dark bands: clouds of dust that hide the stars behind them. This is the best time of year to see it. Its brightest part passes high in the evening sky.
season-constellations.south-winter.cra: South of the Teapot, towards Scorpius’s tail, a small arc of faint stars forms an open crown. This is Corona Australis, discreet but elegant under a dark sky. It is a gauge of your sky: if you see the whole arc, the night is a good one.
season-constellations.south-winter.cra.k: South of the Teapot, towards Scorpius’s tail, a small arc of faint stars forms an open crown: Corona Australis. It is faint but pretty under a dark sky. If you see the whole arc, your sky is very good tonight.
season-constellations.south-winter.ara: Go down towards the south, under the curled tail of Scorpius: a few medium-bright stars form Ara, a small rectangle lying on its side. From mid northern latitudes, Ara stays below the horizon or very nearly so: it is a figure of the southern sky only.
season-constellations.south-winter.ara.k: Go down towards the south, under the curled tail of Scorpius. A few medium-bright stars form Ara, a small rectangle lying on its side. From mid northern latitudes it stays below the horizon, or nearly: it belongs to the southern sky.
season-constellations.south-winter.tra: Further south, between Ara and the Pointers of Centaurus, three fairly bright stars form an almost perfect triangle. This is Triangulum Australe, far sharper than its northern cousin. It is close enough to the pole never to set from mid southern latitudes.
season-constellations.south-winter.tra.k: Further south, between Ara and the Pointers of Centaurus, look for three fairly bright stars. They form an almost perfect triangle: Triangulum Australe. It is so close to the pole that, from mid southern latitudes, it never sets.
season-constellations.south-winter.oph: Go back to the heart of Scorpius and head north, beyond the zenith: a large figure of medium-bright stars, with no very bright star, fills a whole stretch of sky. This is Ophiuchus, the serpent bearer. The Sun passes through it every year in December, even though it is not one of the signs of the zodiac.
season-constellations.south-winter.oph.k: From the heart of Scorpius, go north, beyond the point above your head. A large figure of medium-bright stars fills a wide stretch of sky: Ophiuchus, the serpent bearer. No star in it is very bright. The Sun passes through it every December, even though it is not a sign of the zodiac.
season-constellations.south-winter.aql: Further north, halfway up, a bright star between two fainter ones marks Aquila: this is Altair. With Vega, lower, and Deneb, almost on the northern horizon, it forms the Summer Triangle of the north, which here is a winter landmark. From the southern hemisphere, the Milky Way links Aquila to Scorpius in a single bright band above you.
season-constellations.south-winter.aql.k: Further north, halfway up, a bright star between two fainter ones marks Aquila: this is Altair. With Vega, lower, and Deneb, almost on the northern horizon, it forms the Summer Triangle of the north. Here it is a winter landmark. The Milky Way links Aquila to Scorpius in a single bright band above you.
season-constellations.south-spring.subti: From the south to the north, starting from the Magellanic Clouds.
season-constellations.south-spring.tuc: Facing south, halfway up, two pale patches float apart from the Milky Way; the smaller one, higher tonight, is the Small Magellanic Cloud. Right beside it, a slightly fuzzy star turns into a small bright ball in binoculars, much sharper than the cloud. Faint Tucana is drawn around these two wonders.
season-constellations.south-spring.tuc.k: Facing south, halfway up, two pale patches float apart from the Milky Way. The smaller one, higher tonight, is the Small Magellanic Cloud. Right beside it, a slightly fuzzy star becomes a small bright ball in binoculars, much sharper than the cloud. The faint stars of Tucana are drawn around them.
season-constellations.south-spring.eri: From the Small Cloud, go north for a fist and a half: a bright, isolated star, Achernar, ends a long river of faint stars. This river zigzags up to the north-east, to near Rigel, which rises only later. Eridanus is the sixth largest constellation in the sky.
season-constellations.south-spring.eri.k: From the Small Cloud, go north for a fist and a half. A bright, isolated star, Achernar, ends a long river of faint stars. The river zigzags north-east, almost to Rigel, which rises later. Eridanus is the sixth largest constellation in the sky.
season-constellations.south-spring.phe: Between Achernar and Fomalhaut, almost overhead, a medium-bright star marks Phoenix. In binoculars, its orange colour sets it apart from its white neighbours. The rest of the figure is made of faint stars, which you can follow under a dark sky.
season-constellations.south-spring.phe.k: Between Achernar and Fomalhaut, almost overhead, a medium-bright star marks Phoenix. In binoculars, its orange colour sets it apart from its white neighbours. The rest of the figure is made of faint stars: look for them under a dark sky.
season-constellations.south-spring.gru: Continue towards Fomalhaut, to the west: a long, almost straight line of stars starts from a fairly bright star and stretches towards Tucana. This is Grus, the Crane, with its long neck stretched out. In the middle of the neck, two pairs of close stars split to the naked eye under a good sky: an exercise for your eyes.
season-constellations.south-spring.gru.k: Go towards Fomalhaut, to the west. A long, almost straight line of stars starts from a fairly bright star and stretches towards Tucana. This is Grus, the Crane, with its long neck stretched out. In the middle of the neck, two pairs of close stars split to the naked eye under a good sky. A good exercise for your eyes.
season-constellations.south-spring.psa: Above you, a bright isolated star dominates this star-poor region: Fomalhaut. From here it passes almost through the zenith; from mid northern latitudes, it stays low on the southern horizon.
season-constellations.south-spring.psa.k: Above you, a bright isolated star dominates this star-poor region: Fomalhaut. From here it passes almost overhead. From mid northern latitudes, it stays low on the southern horizon.
season-constellations.south-spring.scl: Between Fomalhaut and Achernar, the region of Sculptor looks empty to the naked eye: none of its stars reaches fourth magnitude. Here we look out of the disc of our galaxy, towards its south pole. In binoculars and telescopes, this void fills with distant galaxies.
season-constellations.south-spring.scl.k: Between Fomalhaut and Achernar, the region of Sculptor looks empty to the naked eye: its stars are all faint. Here we look out of the disc of our galaxy, towards its south pole. In binoculars and telescopes, this void fills with distant galaxies.
season-constellations.south-spring.aqr: Go north from Fomalhaut by an open hand’s width: you enter Aquarius, vast and pale. Its faint stars need a dark sky. In early May, the shooting stars of the Eta Aquariids seem to come from this region: dust left by a famous comet that returns about every 76 years.
season-constellations.south-spring.aqr.k: Go north from Fomalhaut by an open hand’s width: you enter Aquarius, vast and pale. Its faint stars need a dark sky. In early May, the shooting stars of the Eta Aquariids seem to come from here. They are dust from a famous comet that returns about every 76 years.
season-constellations.south-spring.peg: To finish, turn to the north, low on the horizon: four stars of equal brightness form a big square, upside down as seen from here. This is Pegasus, a northern figure that never climbs high from the southern hemisphere. At the same moment, from the north, this square passes high in the sky: it is a landmark common to both hemispheres.
season-constellations.south-spring.peg.k: To finish, turn to the north, low on the horizon. Four stars of equal brightness form a big square, upside down as seen from here. This is Pegasus, a northern figure that never climbs high in the southern sky. At the same moment, from the north, the square passes high: it is a landmark common to both hemispheres.
deep-sky-telescope.title: The deep sky through a telescope
deep-sky-telescope.subtitle: Clusters, nebulae and galaxies, from the easiest to the faintest.
deep-sky-telescope.intro: This tour calls for a telescope with an aperture of 100 to 150 mm. The pointing aid, or a connected GoTo mount, brings each object into the field; without it, each step tells you how to get there from a landmark star. Always start at the lowest magnification, then go higher if the object can take it.
deep-sky-telescope.intro.kids: This tour calls for a telescope with an aperture of 100 to 150 mm. The pointing aid, or a connected GoTo mount, aims the telescope at each object. Without it, each step explains how to find the object from a landmark star. Always start at the lowest magnification.
deep-sky-telescope.outro: Through a telescope, the deep sky does not look like the photographs: the eye sees grey glows, but that light set out thousands or millions of years ago. Each darker night shows more. Note what you saw in the Journal, and come back to the faintest objects on a moonless night.
deep-sky-telescope.outro.kids: Through a telescope, the deep sky does not look like the photographs: the eye sees grey glows. Yet that light set out thousands or millions of years ago. A darker night shows more. Note what you saw in the Journal. Come back to the faintest objects on a moonless night.
deep-sky-telescope.north-winter.subtitle: Around Orion and Gemini, winter clusters and nebulae.
deep-sky-telescope.north-winter.m42: Point at Orion’s sword, below the three belt stars: even under a city sky, a greenish glow shaped like spread wings fills the field. At the centre, raise the magnification: four close stars in a small trapezium light up the whole cloud. It is the ideal first object, because it takes any magnification.
deep-sky-telescope.north-winter.m42.kids: Point at Orion’s sword, below the three belt stars. Even under a city sky, a greenish glow shaped like spread wings fills the field. At the centre, raise the magnification: four close stars in a small trapezium light up the cloud. It is the ideal first object: it looks good at any magnification.
deep-sky-telescope.north-winter.m45: Go up to the Pleiades, above and to the right of Aldebaran, at the lowest magnification: the cluster soon overflows the field. Dozens of bluish stars appear, far more than the naked eye shows. The blue veil seen in photographs, a dust cloud the cluster is passing through, stays almost invisible to the eye.
deep-sky-telescope.north-winter.m45.kids: Go up to the Pleiades, above and to the right of Aldebaran, at the lowest magnification. The cluster soon overflows the field. Dozens of bluish stars appear, far more than the naked eye shows. In photographs a blue veil surrounds them: a dust cloud, almost invisible to the eye.
deep-sky-telescope.north-winter.m37: Go up to Auriga: in the middle of its figure, three open clusters lie in a row, easy to find with the pointing aid. This one, the richest of the three, shows a dusting of fine stars with an orange star near the centre. Compare it with its two neighbours: each has its own character, from the tightest to the loosest.
deep-sky-telescope.north-winter.m37.kids: Go up to Auriga: in the middle of its figure, three open clusters lie in a row. The pointing aid finds them easily. This one is the richest, a dusting of fine stars with an orange star near the centre. Compare it with its two neighbours: each has its own character, from the tightest to the loosest.
deep-sky-telescope.north-winter.m35: At the foot of Gemini, near the westernmost star of the figure, a large cluster is already visible in the finderscope. Through the telescope, a hundred or so stars spread out in arcs and chains. Right beside it, a small tight patch is another, much more distant cluster, whose stars melt into a glow.
deep-sky-telescope.north-winter.m35.kids: At the foot of Gemini, near the westernmost star of the figure, a large cluster is already visible in the finderscope. Through the telescope, a hundred or so stars spread out in arcs and chains. Right beside it, a small tight patch is another cluster, much more distant. Its stars melt into a glow.
deep-sky-telescope.north-winter.ngc-2392: Follow the line of stars running down from Pollux towards Orion as far as its middle: very close by, a small star looks fuzzy. At 100× or more, it becomes a small blue-green disc with a star at its centre, the one that blew off this shell of gas. That central star is easy to see, which is rare for a planetary nebula.

Follow the line of stars running down from Pollux towards Orion as far as its middle. Very close by, a small star looks fuzzy. At 100× or more, it is a small blue-green disc with a star at its centre. That star blew off this shell of gas. It is easy to see, which is rare for a planetary nebula.
deep-sky-telescope.north-winter.ngc-2244: Go back to Betelgeuse and move about a fist to the east: a loose cluster of six bright stars in a rectangle shows at the lowest magnification. Around it, the great Rosette Nebula stays invisible under an average sky; a nebula filter brings out patches of it. This is a very young cluster, born from that cloud a few million years ago.

Go back to Betelgeuse and move about a fist to the east. At the lowest magnification, six bright stars form a rectangle: a loose cluster. The Rosette Nebula around it stays invisible under an average sky. This cluster is very young: it was born from that cloud a few million years ago.
deep-sky-telescope.north-winter.m41: Go down below Sirius, less than a fist to the south: this cluster is bright enough to be seen with the naked eye under a truly dark sky. Through the telescope it shows dozens of stars, including an orange one near the centre. It is low from mid northern latitudes: aim at it when it is due south.
deep-sky-telescope.north-winter.m41.kids: Go down below Sirius, less than a fist to the south. This cluster is bright enough to see with the naked eye under a truly dark sky. Through the telescope, you see dozens of stars, including an orange one near the centre. It is low from mid northern latitudes: aim at it when it is due south.
deep-sky-telescope.north-winter.m46: Go one and a half fists east of Sirius: a cluster rich in faint stars looks like spilled salt at medium magnification. On its edge, a small grey bubble is a planetary nebula lying in front of the cluster, unrelated to it. Just to the west, a neighbouring cluster, brighter and looser, provides the contrast.
deep-sky-telescope.north-winter.m46.kids: Go one and a half fists east of Sirius. A cluster rich in faint stars looks like spilled salt at medium magnification. On its edge, a small grey bubble is a planetary nebula in front of the cluster, unrelated to it. Just to the west, a neighbouring cluster, brighter and looser, makes a nice contrast.
deep-sky-telescope.north-spring.subtitle: From Cancer to Virgo, the galaxies of spring.
deep-sky-telescope.north-spring.m44: Start at the heart of Cancer, at the lowest magnification: the Beehive Cluster is three times wider than the full Moon. Dozens of stars are scattered across it, several of them orange. It is a good object for setting the focus before the fainter galaxies.
deep-sky-telescope.north-spring.m44.kids: Start at the heart of Cancer, at the lowest magnification. The Beehive Cluster is three times wider than the full Moon. Dozens of stars are scattered across it, several of them orange. It is ideal for setting the focus before you try the fainter galaxies.
deep-sky-telescope.north-spring.m81: Go up to Ursa Major and extend the diagonal of the Big Dipper’s bowl beyond its north-west corner: two galaxies fit in the same field at low magnification. The brighter one is an oval with a well-marked core; the other is an elongated spindle, with dark streaks for a patient eye. This pair is often the first galaxy people see without any hesitation.
deep-sky-telescope.north-spring.m81.kids: Go up to Ursa Major and extend the diagonal of the Big Dipper’s bowl beyond its north-west corner. Two galaxies fit in the same field at low magnification. The brighter one is an oval with a clear core. The other is a long spindle, with dark streaks for a patient eye. These two are often the first galaxies people are sure they have seen.
deep-sky-telescope.north-spring.mizar: Go back to the middle of the Big Dipper’s handle, to Mizar, which has Alcor beside it to the naked eye. From 50×, Mizar clearly splits into two white stars. It was the first pair of stars discovered with a telescope, about four centuries ago.
deep-sky-telescope.north-spring.mizar.ki: Go back to the middle of the Big Dipper’s handle, to Mizar. Alcor is beside it to the naked eye. From 50×, Mizar clearly splits into two white stars. It was the first pair of stars found with a telescope, about four centuries ago.
deep-sky-telescope.north-spring.m51: From the star at the end of the handle, go down half a fist to the south-west: two round patches, one large and one small, almost touch. Under an average sky you mainly see their two cores; under a truly dark sky, with a 150 mm telescope, you can just make out the spiral of the larger one. Look a little to the side of the object: the edge of the eye is more sensitive to faint light.
deep-sky-telescope.north-spring.m51.kids: From the star at the end of the handle, go down half a fist to the south-west. Two round patches, one large and one small, almost touch. Under an average sky you mainly see their two cores. Under a dark sky, with a 150 mm telescope, you can just see the large one’s spiral. Look a little to the side of the object: the edge of your eye sees faint light better.
deep-sky-telescope.north-spring.m3: A little over a fist to the north-west of Arcturus, a fuzzy star appears in the finderscope: a globular cluster. Through the telescope, it is a bright ball whose edges break into tiny stars at high magnification. It holds about half a million stars.
deep-sky-telescope.north-spring.m3.kids: A little over a fist to the north-west of Arcturus, a fuzzy star appears in the finderscope: a globular cluster, a ball of stars. At high magnification, its edges break into tiny stars. It holds about half a million stars.
deep-sky-telescope.north-spring.m65: Move on to Leo: under the hind part of the body, between the two stars of the thigh, three galaxies fit in one wide field. Two elongated ovals are easy to see; the third, seen edge-on, is a pale streak that needs a dark sky. Moving the telescope slightly helps the eye pick up the faintest glows.
deep-sky-telescope.north-spring.m65.kids: Move on to Leo: under the hind part of the body, between the two stars of the thigh, three galaxies fit in one wide field. Two elongated ovals are easy to see. The third, seen edge-on, is a pale streak that needs a dark sky. Move the telescope very slightly: the eye spots faint glows better.
deep-sky-telescope.north-spring.ngc-2903: Go back to Leo’s head, at the end of its curve of stars: just to the south, a faint, elongated galaxy waits. It is brighter than many galaxies in the famous 18th-century catalogue, which nevertheless left it out. Under an average sky, it is a grey oval with a slightly brighter centre.

Go back to Leo’s head, at the end of its curve of stars. Just to the south, a faint, elongated galaxy waits. It is brighter than many galaxies in a famous 18th-century catalogue, which left it out. Under an average sky, it is a grey oval.
deep-sky-telescope.north-spring.ngc-3242: Go far south, under Crater, into Hydra: a small bluish star looks fuzzy. At 100× and more, a blue-green disc appears, surrounded by a paler ring: it is called the Ghost of Jupiter, because its apparent size is close to that of the planet. It takes magnification well, even under a city sky.

Go far south, under Crater, into Hydra. A small bluish star looks fuzzy. At 100× and more, a blue-green disc appears, ringed by a paler halo. It is the Ghost of Jupiter: in the sky, it looks about as big as the planet. It stays sharp at high magnification, even under a city sky.
deep-sky-telescope.north-spring.m104: To finish, between Spica and Corvus, nearer Corvus, a galaxy seen almost edge-on looks like a bright spindle. With a 150 mm telescope, a thin dark band cuts it lengthwise, like the brim of a hat. It is bright enough to be seen under an average sky.
deep-sky-telescope.north-spring.m104.kid: To finish, between Spica and Corvus, nearer Corvus, look for a galaxy seen almost edge-on. It looks like a bright spindle. With a 150 mm telescope, a thin dark band cuts it lengthwise, like the brim of a hat. It shows even under an average sky.
deep-sky-telescope.north-summer.subtitle: From Hercules to Sagittarius, clusters, nebulae and bubbles of gas.
deep-sky-telescope.north-summer.m13: Start with Hercules: on the west side of the trapezium, a third of the way along from the top, a fuzzy star is already visible in the finderscope. Through the telescope, it becomes a ball of light whose edges break into hundreds of stars at 100×. Take your time: the longer the eye adapts, the more the centre resolves.
deep-sky-telescope.north-summer.m13.kids: Start with Hercules. On the west side of the trapezium, a third of the way along from the top, a fuzzy star is already visible in the finderscope. Through the telescope, it is a ball of light. At 100×, its edges break into hundreds of stars. The longer your eye adapts, the more you see towards the centre.
deep-sky-telescope.north-summer.m57: Move on to Lyra: halfway between the two bottom stars of the small parallelogram, a tiny smoke ring floats. Raise the magnification to 100×: it becomes a grey oval with a darker centre, like a doughnut. The star at its centre is too faint for a telescope of this size.
deep-sky-telescope.north-summer.m57.kids: Move on to Lyra. Halfway between the two bottom stars of the small parallelogram, a tiny smoke ring floats. At 100×, it is a grey oval with a darker centre, like a doughnut. The star at its centre is too faint for a telescope of this size.
deep-sky-telescope.north-summer.ngc-6543: Go up to Draco, halfway between Vega and the pole star: the pointing aid is welcome, because the region has few landmarks. A small, fuzzy blue-green star holds up under magnification: push it to 150×. Its colour is easier to see than that of most nebulae, which makes it easy despite its small size.

Go up to Draco, halfway between Vega and the pole star. There are few landmarks, so the pointing aid is useful. A small, fuzzy blue-green star can take a lot of magnification: push it to 150×. Its colour is easier to see than that of most nebulae.
deep-sky-telescope.north-summer.ngc-6826: Come back down to Cygnus, near the tip of its west wing: a small bluish nebula surrounds a fairly bright star. Look at the star directly, then beside it: the nebula disappears and reappears, hence its nickname, the Blinking Planetary. This little game clearly shows the difference between direct vision and averted vision.

Come back down to Cygnus, near the tip of its west wing. A small bluish nebula surrounds a fairly bright star. Look at the star directly, then beside it: the nebula disappears, then comes back. It is called the Blinking Planetary. This game shows the difference between looking straight at something and looking beside it.
deep-sky-telescope.north-summer.m27: Go north of Altair, just above the tip of Sagitta: a rectangular glow, a quarter of the full Moon’s diameter across, is visible in the finderscope. Through the telescope, it takes the shape of an apple core or an hourglass. It is the easiest of the planetary nebulae, even under a suburban sky.
deep-sky-telescope.north-summer.m27.kids: Go north of Altair, just above the tip of Sagitta. A rectangular glow, a quarter of the full Moon’s diameter across, shows in the finderscope. Through the telescope, it looks like an apple core or an hourglass. It is the easiest planetary nebula, even from the suburbs.
deep-sky-telescope.north-summer.m11: Follow the Eagle’s tail to the south-west as far as Scutum, in the Milky Way: a very rich fan-shaped cluster, with a bright star at its tip, is visible in the finderscope. Through the telescope, it resolves into hundreds of crowded stars. Amateurs call it the Wild Duck Cluster: its stars recall a V-shaped flight of ducks.
deep-sky-telescope.north-summer.m11.kids: Follow the Eagle’s tail to the south-west as far as Scutum, in the Milky Way. A very rich fan-shaped cluster, with a bright star at its tip, shows in the finderscope. Through the telescope, hundreds of crowded stars appear. It is called the Wild Duck Cluster: its stars recall a V-shaped flight of ducks.
deep-sky-telescope.north-summer.m17: Keep going south along the Milky Way: a bright nebula shaped like a swan, or a number 2, floats in a very starry field. Under an average sky, its bright bar is visible without a filter; a nebula filter brings out the curved neck. It is bright enough to be seen from the suburbs.
deep-sky-telescope.north-summer.m17.kids: Keep going south along the Milky Way. A bright nebula shaped like a swan, or a number 2, floats in a very starry field. Under an average sky, its bright bar shows without a filter. A nebula filter brings out the curved neck. You can see it even from the suburbs.
deep-sky-telescope.north-summer.m8: Lower down, above the spout of the Teapot, a large elongated glow contains a star cluster: the Lagoon Nebula. A dark lane splits it in two, hence its name. It is low from mid northern latitudes: aim at it when it is due south, early in the evening.
deep-sky-telescope.north-summer.m8.kids: Lower down, above the spout of the Teapot, a large elongated glow holds a star cluster: the Lagoon Nebula. A dark lane splits it in two, hence its name. It is low from mid northern latitudes. Aim at it when it is due south, early in the evening.
deep-sky-telescope.north-summer.m22: Just above the lid of the Teapot, a bright globular cluster is visible in the finderscope, larger than the one in Hercules. Through the telescope, it breaks into stars more easily, because its stars are brighter. It is one of the globular clusters closest to us.
deep-sky-telescope.north-summer.m22.kids: Just above the lid of the Teapot, a bright globular cluster shows in the finderscope. It is larger than the one in Hercules. Its brighter stars separate more easily. It is one of the globular clusters closest to us.
deep-sky-telescope.north-autumn.subtitle: From Pegasus to Perseus, galaxies, clusters and double stars.
deep-sky-telescope.north-autumn.m15: Start from the star marking the nose of Pegasus and go half a fist to the north-west: a fuzzy star appears in the finderscope. Through the telescope, it is a globular cluster with a very tight core, more concentrated than most. It hosts one of the few planetary nebulae known in a globular cluster, though that is out of reach of a small telescope.
deep-sky-telescope.north-autumn.m15.kids: Start from the star marking the nose of Pegasus and go half a fist to the north-west. A fuzzy star appears in the finderscope. Through the telescope, it is a globular cluster with a very tight core. It hosts one of the few planetary nebulae known in a globular cluster, but a small telescope will not show it.
deep-sky-telescope.north-autumn.ngc-7662: Move to the west of the Andromeda chain, near a small triangle of faint stars: a bluish star looks bigger than the others. At 150×, it is a small blue disc, hence its nickname, the Blue Snowball. Its colour is easy to see, even under a city sky.

Move to the west of the Andromeda chain, near a small triangle of faint stars. A bluish star looks bigger than the others. At 150×, it is a small blue disc: the Blue Snowball. Its colour is easy to see, even under a city sky.
deep-sky-telescope.north-autumn.m31: Point at the Andromeda Galaxy, north of Mirach, at the lowest magnification: it spills well beyond the field. The core is an intense oval glow; two small galaxies accompany it, one round and very close, the other oval and fainter. Under an average sky, do not expect a spiral: sweep slowly to get a feel for the extent of the disc.
deep-sky-telescope.north-autumn.m31.kids: Point at the Andromeda Galaxy, north of Mirach, at the lowest magnification. It spills well beyond the field. The core is an oval glow. Two small galaxies accompany it, one round and very close, the other oval and fainter. Under an average sky, do not expect a spiral. Sweep slowly to get a feel for how big the disc is.
deep-sky-telescope.north-autumn.almach: Go back to the Andromeda chain, to its easternmost star, Almach. At 50× or more, a small companion appears right against the main star. The colour contrast shows better if you raise the magnification a little and let your eye rest between glances.
deep-sky-telescope.north-autumn.almach.k: Go back to the Andromeda chain, to its easternmost star, Almach. At 50× or more, a small companion appears right against the main star. To see the colours better, raise the magnification a little and let your eye rest between glances.
deep-sky-telescope.north-autumn.m33: Go back to Mirach and cross over to Triangulum: halfway, a large, very faint glow, wider than the full Moon, needs a dark sky. At the lowest magnification, sweep slowly: it shows up by contrast, as a lighter patch of the sky background. Under a city sky it can stay invisible, whereas binoculars show it under a truly dark sky.
deep-sky-telescope.north-autumn.m33.kids: Go back to Mirach and cross over to Triangulum. Halfway, a large, very faint glow, wider than the full Moon, needs a dark sky. At the lowest magnification, sweep slowly: it shows up by contrast, as a patch a bit lighter than the sky. Under a city sky it can stay invisible. Binoculars show it under a truly dark sky.
deep-sky-telescope.north-autumn.ngc-457: Go up to Cassiopeia, just south of the fourth star of the W counting from the west: a cluster is shaped like an owl with its wings spread, with two brighter stars for the eyes. A hundred or so stars show through the telescope. Amateurs also call it the E.T. Cluster, for its resemblance to a film character.
Go up to Cassiopeia, just south of the fourth star of the W counting from the west. This cluster is shaped like an owl with its wings spread, with two brighter stars for the eyes. About a hundred stars show through the telescope. Some people call it the E.T. Cluster, because it looks like a film character.
deep-sky-telescope.north-autumn.ngc-869: Go down from Cassiopeia towards Perseus, halfway: the glow that the naked eye can just make out splits into two clusters side by side in the finderscope. At the lowest magnification, both fit in the same field, sprinkled with bluish stars and a few orange ones. It is one of the finest sights for a small telescope.
Go down from Cassiopeia towards Perseus, halfway. The glow your naked eye can just make out splits into two clusters side by side in the finderscope. Both fit in the same field, sprinkled with bluish stars and a few orange ones. It is a fine sight for a small telescope.
deep-sky-telescope.north-autumn.ngc-253: To finish, look low to the south, a fist south of Diphda, in Cetus: a large, elongated galaxy, seen almost edge-on, is visible in the finderscope. Through the telescope, it is a mottled spindle, bright along its whole length. From mid northern latitudes it stays low: aim at it when it is due south, with a clear horizon.
To finish, look low to the south, a fist south of Diphda, in Cetus. A large, elongated galaxy, seen almost edge-on, shows in the finderscope. Through the telescope, it is a mottled spindle, bright along its whole length. From mid northern latitudes it stays low: aim at it when it is due south.
deep-sky-telescope.south-summer.subtitle: Orion upside down, Puppis and the Large Magellanic Cloud.
deep-sky-telescope.south-summer.m42: Point at Orion’s sword, above the three belt stars as seen from here: even under a city sky, a glow like spread wings fills the field. At the centre, raise the magnification: four close stars forming a tiny Trapezium light up the cloud. From the south, the nebula passes high in the sky, far from the unsteady air of the horizon.
deep-sky-telescope.south-summer.m42.kids: Point at Orion’s sword, above the three belt stars as seen from here. Even under a city sky, a glow like spread wings fills the field. At the centre, raise the magnification: four close stars forming a tiny trapezium light up the cloud. From the south, the nebula passes high, far from the unsteady air of the horizon.
deep-sky-telescope.south-summer.m45: Low to the north, the Pleiades are best viewed at the lowest magnification, because the cluster soon overflows the field. Dozens of bluish stars appear that the naked eye did not show. Aim at them early in the evening, before they set in the north-west.
deep-sky-telescope.south-summer.m45.kids: Low to the north, look at the Pleiades at the lowest magnification, because the cluster soon overflows the field. Dozens of bluish stars appear, too faint for the naked eye. Aim at them early in the evening, before they set in the north-west.
deep-sky-telescope.south-summer.ngc-1851: Move to Columba, to the south-west of its main star: a fuzzy star appears in the finderscope. Through the telescope, it is a small but very bright globular cluster, with a tight core like a lighthouse. From mid northern latitudes it hardly rises at all: it is an object of the southern sky.

Move to Columba, to the south-west of its main star. A fuzzy star appears in the finderscope. Through the telescope, it is a small but very bright globular cluster, with a tight core like a lighthouse. From mid northern latitudes it hardly rises at all: it belongs to the southern sky.
