deep-sky-telescope.south-summer.m41: Less than a fist south of Sirius, almost at the zenith, a bright cluster is visible to the naked eye under a truly dark sky. Through the telescope it shows dozens of stars, including an orange one near the centre. Here it passes high, whereas from the north it stays low on the horizon.
deep-sky-telescope.south-summer.m41.kids: Less than a fist south of Sirius, almost at the zenith, a bright cluster shines. Under a truly dark sky you can see it with the naked eye. Through the telescope you see dozens of stars, including an orange one. Here it passes high, whereas from the north it stays low.
deep-sky-telescope.south-summer.m46: One and a half fists east of Sirius, a cluster rich in faint stars looks like spilled salt. On its edge, a small grey bubble is a planetary nebula, lying in front of the cluster and unrelated to it. Its neighbour to the west, brighter and looser, provides the contrast.
deep-sky-telescope.south-summer.m46.kids: Go one and a half fists east of Sirius. A cluster rich in faint stars looks like spilled salt. On its edge, a small grey bubble is a planetary nebula in front of the cluster, unrelated to it. Its brighter neighbour to the west makes a nice contrast.
deep-sky-telescope.south-summer.ngc-2477: Continue south, in Puppis, near its brightest star: a round, tight cluster is visible in the finderscope. Through the telescope, hundreds of fine stars of equal brightness fill the field like a globular cluster coming apart. It is one of the richest open clusters in the sky.

Continue south, in Puppis, near its brightest star. A round, tight cluster shows in the finderscope. Through the telescope, hundreds of fine stars of equal brightness fill the field, like a globular cluster coming apart. It is one of the richest open clusters in the sky.
deep-sky-telescope.south-summer.ngc-2516: Further south, in Carina, near Avior, a large bright cluster is visible to the naked eye under a truly dark sky. At the lowest magnification, a hundred or so stars, a few of them orange, trace chains and curves. It is sometimes nicknamed the Southern Beehive.

Further south, in Carina, near Avior, a large bright cluster can be seen with the naked eye under a truly dark sky. At the lowest magnification, a hundred or so stars, a few orange, trace chains and curves. It is sometimes called the Southern Beehive.
deep-sky-telescope.south-summer.ngc-2070: To finish, go back to the Large Magellanic Cloud: on its eastern edge, a glow stands out, visible even in binoculars. Through the telescope, the Tarantula Nebula spreads filaments like legs around a bright core. If it were as close as the Orion Nebula, it would light up the night enough to cast shadows.

To finish, go back to the Large Magellanic Cloud. On its eastern edge, a glow stands out, visible even in binoculars. Through the telescope, the Tarantula Nebula spreads filaments like legs around a bright core. If it were as close as the Orion Nebula, it would light up the night enough to cast shadows.
deep-sky-telescope.south-autumn.subtitle: From Carina to Centaurus, in the heart of the southern Milky Way.
deep-sky-telescope.south-autumn.ngc-3242: Start in Hydra, under Crater: a small bluish star looks fuzzy. At 100× and more, a blue-green disc surrounded by a paler ring appears, the Ghost of Jupiter, as large in the sky as the planet. From here it passes high in the sky and takes magnification well.

Start in Hydra, under Crater. A small bluish star looks fuzzy. At 100× and more, a blue-green disc with a paler ring appears: the Ghost of Jupiter, as large in the sky as the planet. From here it passes high and stays sharp at high magnification.
deep-sky-telescope.south-autumn.ngc-3532: Slide over to Carina, along the Milky Way, west of the Cross: a large cluster, visible to the naked eye, fills the field at the lowest magnification. Hundreds of stars trace arcs and chains, with a few orange ones. It is one of the finest open clusters in the whole sky.

Slide over to Carina, along the Milky Way, west of the Cross. A large cluster, visible to the naked eye, fills the field at the lowest magnification. Hundreds of stars trace arcs and chains, with a few orange ones. It is one of the finest open clusters in the sky.
deep-sky-telescope.south-autumn.ngc-3372: Right next to it, to the west, a vast nebula is visible to the naked eye; at the lowest magnification, it spills beyond the field. Dark lanes cut across it; at the centre, a black keyhole-shaped patch sits beside the orange star Eta Carinae. A nebula filter reveals even more.

Right next to it, to the west, you can see a vast nebula with the naked eye. At the lowest magnification, it spills beyond the field. Dark lanes cut across it. At the centre, a black keyhole-shaped patch sits beside the orange star Eta Carinae. A nebula filter shows more.
deep-sky-telescope.south-autumn.acrux: Move to the Southern Cross, to the star at the foot, Acrux. From 50×, it splits into two very close, almost equal blue-white stars. It is one of the finest double stars of the southern sky.
deep-sky-telescope.south-autumn.acrux.ki: Move to the Southern Cross, to the star at the foot: Acrux. From 50×, it splits into two very close, almost equal blue-white stars. It is one of the finest double stars of the south.
deep-sky-telescope.south-autumn.ngc-4755: Go back up to the left-hand star of the Cross, Mimosa: right next to it, a small tight cluster is visible in the finderscope. Through the telescope, an orange star shines among blue-white ones, as if in a jewel case. The nearby Coalsack gives a black background that makes the cluster stand out.

Go back up to the left-hand star of the Cross, Mimosa. Right next to it, a small tight cluster shows in the finderscope. Through the telescope, an orange star shines among blue-white ones, like a jewel. The nearby Coalsack gives a black background that makes the cluster stand out.
deep-sky-telescope.south-autumn.ngc-5139: Go back up to Centaurus: the fuzzy ball seen with the naked eye becomes a huge swarm through the telescope, wider than half the full Moon. Thousands of stars resolve from medium magnification, right to the centre. For a small telescope, no other globular cluster comes close.

Go back up to Centaurus. To the naked eye it is a fuzzy ball. Through the telescope, it is a huge swarm, wider than half the full Moon. At medium magnification, it breaks into thousands of separate stars. For a small telescope, no other globular cluster comes close.
deep-sky-telescope.south-autumn.ngc-5128: Half a fist north of Omega Centauri, a bright round galaxy is cut in two by a broad dark band. Even with a 100 mm telescope, the band is easy to see under a decent sky. It is one of the strangest galaxies in the sky: a giant black hole makes it one of the most powerful radio sources.

Half a fist north of Omega Centauri, a bright round galaxy is cut in two by a broad dark band. Even with a 100 mm telescope, you can see the band under a decent sky. It is one of the strangest galaxies. A giant black hole makes it one of the most powerful radio sources.
deep-sky-telescope.south-autumn.m83: Go north by an open hand’s width, on the border of Hydra and Centaurus: a galaxy seen face-on, with a bright core, is visible in the finderscope. With a 150 mm telescope, you can just make out a central bar and the start of the arms. It is nicknamed the Southern Pinwheel.
deep-sky-telescope.south-autumn.m83.kids: Go north by an open hand’s width, on the border of Hydra and Centaurus. A galaxy seen face-on, with a bright core, shows in the finderscope. With a 150 mm telescope, you can just make out a central bar and the start of the arms. It is the Southern Pinwheel.
deep-sky-telescope.south-autumn.m104: To finish, between Spica and Corvus, nearer Corvus, a galaxy seen almost edge-on looks like a bright spindle. With a 150 mm telescope, a thin dark band cuts it lengthwise. Its nickname, the Sombrero, comes from that hat shape.
deep-sky-telescope.south-autumn.m104.kid: To finish, between Spica and Corvus, nearer Corvus, look for a galaxy seen almost edge-on. It looks like a bright spindle. With a 150 mm telescope, a thin dark band cuts it in two. It is the Sombrero, named for its hat shape.
deep-sky-telescope.south-winter.subtitle: Scorpius and Sagittarius at the zenith, the heart of the Milky Way.
deep-sky-telescope.south-winter.ngc-6231: Start in the tail of Scorpius, near the orange and blue pair of stars in its curve: a tight cluster of bright stars is visible to the naked eye. Through the telescope, a handful of very young blue stars shine like diamonds. With the neighbouring stars, it forms a trail, hence its nickname, the False Comet.

Start in the tail of Scorpius, near the orange and blue pair of stars in its curve. A tight cluster of bright stars shows to the naked eye. Through the telescope, a handful of very young blue stars shine like diamonds. With the neighbouring stars, it makes a trail: it is called the False Comet.
deep-sky-telescope.south-winter.m4: Go back to Antares: just to the west, in the same finderscope field, a round, pale patch is a globular cluster. Through the telescope, it breaks into stars easily, crossed at its centre by a bar of stars. It is one of the globular clusters closest to us.
deep-sky-telescope.south-winter.m4.kids: Go back to Antares. Just to the west, in the same finderscope field, a round, pale patch is a globular cluster. Through the telescope, its stars separate easily, and a bar of stars crosses its centre. It is one of the globular clusters closest to us.
deep-sky-telescope.south-winter.m6: Go to the sting of Scorpius: north-east of the tail, two bright clusters are visible to the naked eye. The smaller one, through the telescope, looks like a butterfly with open wings, with an orange star on one wing. The second is the next stop.
deep-sky-telescope.south-winter.m6.kids: Go to the sting of Scorpius: north-east of the tail, two bright clusters show to the naked eye. Through the telescope, the smaller one looks like a butterfly with open wings. An orange star sits on one wing. The other is the next stop.
deep-sky-telescope.south-winter.m7: Right next to it, to the south-east, the second cluster is much bigger: at the lowest magnification, dozens of bright stars spill beyond the field. It was already noted in Antiquity, as a small cloud near the sting of Scorpius. In binoculars, it is perhaps even more beautiful than through the telescope.
deep-sky-telescope.south-winter.m7.kids: Right next to it, to the south-east, the second cluster is much bigger. At the lowest magnification, dozens of bright stars spill beyond the field. People already noticed it in ancient times, as a small cloud. In binoculars, it is perhaps even more beautiful than through the telescope.
deep-sky-telescope.south-winter.ngc-6397: Go down to the south, into Ara: a loose, fairly bright globular cluster is visible in the finderscope. Its stars separate even at low magnification, in chains running out from the centre. Its very tight core contrasts with its scattered edges.

deep-sky-telescope.south-winter.m8: Come back to Sagittarius, near the spout of the Teapot: a large elongated glow, with a star cluster, is visible to the naked eye under a truly dark sky. A dark lane splits it in two; a nebula filter reveals its details. Just to the north, a smaller nebula, cut in three by dark lanes, sometimes fits in the same field.

deep-sky-telescope.south-winter.m22: Near the lid of the Teapot, a bright, broad globular cluster is visible in the finderscope. Its stars resolve more easily than those of most globular clusters, because it is close. From here it passes almost through the zenith: this is the time for high magnification.
deep-sky-telescope.south-winter.m22.kids: Near the lid of the Teapot, a bright, broad globular cluster shows in the finderscope. It is close, so its stars separate more easily than in most globular clusters. From here it passes almost overhead: use high magnification.
deep-sky-telescope.south-winter.m17: Follow the Milky Way to the north: a bright nebula shaped like a swan, or a number 2, floats in a very starry field. Its bright bar is visible without a filter; a nebula filter brings out the curved neck. Just to the north, the Eagle Nebula surrounds a cluster, but its famous pillars stay out of the eye’s reach.
deep-sky-telescope.south-winter.m17.kids: Follow the Milky Way to the north. A bright nebula shaped like a swan, or a number 2, floats in a very starry field. Its bright bar shows without a filter. Just to the north, the Eagle Nebula surrounds a cluster, but its famous pillars are too faint for the eye.
deep-sky-telescope.south-winter.m11: Continue north, into Scutum: a very rich fan-shaped cluster, with a bright star at its tip, is visible in the finderscope. Through the telescope, hundreds of crowded stars recall a flight of ducks: it is nicknamed the Wild Duck Cluster. It is one of the richest open clusters known.

deep-sky-telescope.south-winter.ngc-6752: To finish, go far south, a fist west of Peacock, the main star of Pavo: a bright globular cluster is visible in the finderscope. Through the telescope, a dense core is surrounded by a wide halo of stars that resolve well. It is the third brightest globular cluster in the sky, after Omega Centauri and 47 Tucanae.

deep-sky-telescope.south-spring.subtitle: From Aquarius to Tucana, as far as the Small Magellanic Cloud.
deep-sky-telescope.south-spring.ngc-7009: Start in the west of Aquarius: a small, green, fuzzy star holds up under magnification, the Saturn Nebula. At 150×, it is a bright green oval; with a 150 mm telescope and a steady sky, two small handles on either side give it the look of the planet. Its colour is easier to see than that of most nebulae.

Start in the west of Aquarius. A small, green, fuzzy star takes magnification well: the Saturn Nebula. At 150×, it is a bright green oval. With a 150 mm telescope and a steady sky, two small handles on either side make it look like the planet. Its colour is easy to see.
deep-sky-telescope.south-spring.m2: Half a fist north of the brightest star of Aquarius, a fuzzy star is visible in the finderscope: a globular cluster. Through the telescope, it is a dense, bright ball whose edges break into stars at high magnification. It holds about 150,000 stars.
deep-sky-telescope.south-spring.m2.kids: Half a fist north of the brightest star of Aquarius, a fuzzy star shows in the finderscope: a globular cluster. Through the telescope, it is a dense, bright ball whose edges break into stars at high magnification. It holds about 150,000 stars.
deep-sky-telescope.south-spring.ngc-7293: Go down towards Fomalhaut, a fist north of the star: a very large, round, faint glow, half the width of the full Moon, needs a dark sky. At the lowest magnification, with a nebula filter if possible, a thick ring takes shape. It is one of the nearest planetary nebulae: its extent makes it faint, despite its total brightness.

deep-sky-telescope.south-spring.ngc-253: Move to Sculptor, a fist south of Diphda, the brightest star of Cetus: a large, elongated galaxy is visible in the finderscope, and even in binoculars. Through the telescope, it is a mottled spindle, bright along its whole length. From here it passes almost through the zenith: it is one of the finest galaxies for a small telescope.

deep-sky-telescope.south-spring.ngc-288: Very close by, south-east of the galaxy, a faint, loose globular cluster needs a dark sky. Its stars separate at high magnification, without a well-marked core. It lies near the south pole of our galaxy, far from the Milky Way.

deep-sky-telescope.south-spring.ngc-55: Go down to the south, on the border of Sculptor and Phoenix: a very elongated galaxy, seen edge-on, looks like a long bright streak. Through the telescope, it is brighter on one side than the other. With the Sculptor Galaxy, it belongs to a small group of galaxies near our own.

deep-sky-telescope.south-spring.ngc-104: Go down to Tucana: next to the Small Cloud, the fuzzy star seen with the naked eye becomes a dazzling globular cluster through the telescope. Its very concentrated core bursts into thousands of stars from medium magnification. With Omega Centauri, it is one of the two finest globular clusters in the sky.

deep-sky-telescope.south-spring.ngc-362: On the north edge of the Small Cloud, another, smaller globular cluster seems to be part of it. In reality, it is much closer to us than the Cloud. Through the telescope, it is a bright ball with a tight core, which breaks into stars at high magnification.

deep-sky-telescope.south-spring.ngc-292: To finish, take the lowest magnification and wander through the Small Cloud itself: a whole galaxy, about 200,000 light-years away. The field teems with clusters and small nebulae, like brighter grains. Go round it slowly: every corner shows a new object.
